## Further Reading

Balakrishnan, R., Labro, E., & Sivaramakrishnan, K. (2012a). Product costs as decision aids: An analysis of alternative approaches (Part 1). *Accounting Horizons*, *26*(1), 1–20. <https://doi.org/10.2308/acch-50086> The first of two papers that set four ways of computing product costs on one platform: traditional volume-based systems, activity-based costing, time-driven activity-based costing, and resource consumption accounting. A continuing numerical example shows what the systems share and where they differ, much as this case set three costing views side by side.

Balakrishnan, R., Labro, E., & Sivaramakrishnan, K. (2012b). Product costs as decision aids: An analysis of alternative approaches (Part 2). *Accounting Horizons*, *26*(1), 21–41. <https://doi.org/10.2308/acch-10197> The second paper compares the four systems on what they cost to build and maintain, on whether they provide data relevant to decisions, and on the incentives they create to manage the demand for resources. No system dominates, and the authors suggest how future systems might combine the best features of each.

Everaert, P., Bruggeman, W., Sarens, G., Anderson, S. R., & Levant, Y. (2008). Cost modeling in logistics using time-driven ABC: Experiences from a wholesaler. *International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management*, *38*(3), 172–191. <https://doi.org/10.1108/09600030810866977> A case study of time-driven activity-based costing at a Belgian wholesaler, where time equations captured operations that a single cost driver could not. At the case company the time-driven model gave more accurate costs than conventional activity-based costing, and its users found it useful for profitability reporting, which makes it a practical companion to Requirement 4.

Kaplan, R. S., & Anderson, S. R. (2004). Time-driven activity-based costing. *Harvard Business Review*, *82*(11), 131–138. <https://hbr.org/2004/11/time-driven-activity-based-costing> The article that introduced time-driven activity-based costing: estimate the cost of supplying each unit of capacity and the time each product, order, or customer uses, and report the capacity left unused. It is the source of the rule of thumb that practical capacity is 80% to 85% of theoretical capacity.

Marn, M. V., & Rosiello, R. L. (1992). Managing price, gaining profit. *Harvard Business Review*, *70*(5), 84–93. <https://hbr.org/1992/09/managing-price-gaining-profit> A classic on price management. Using the average economics of more than two thousand companies, the authors show that a 1% gain in price raises operating profit more than a 1% gain in volume or a 1% cut in cost, and they trace the pocket price waterfall from the list price to the price a company finally keeps. It frames the repricing decision of Requirement 8.

Noreen, E. (1991). Conditions under which activity-based cost systems provide relevant costs. *Journal of Management Accounting Research*, *3*, 159–168. <https://doi.org/10.2308/jmar-9701273049> A short analytical paper that sets out when activity-based costs are relevant to a decision: each cost pool must depend on a single activity, its cost must be strictly proportional to that activity, and activities must not be shared in joint processes. Committed capacity costs, such as the crew in this case, fail the second condition, which is why the make-or-buy decision rests on relevant costs rather than on any full product cost.
